title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Silence fell over the room. The countess looked at her guests with a pleasant smile, though she made no effort to hide the fact that she wouldn't be upset if they got up and left. The visitor's daughter was already smoothing down her dress and glancing at her mother when suddenly, from the next room, came the sound of boys and girls running toward the door, a chair toppling over, and a thirteen-year-old girl burst in, clutching something hidden in the folds of her short muslin dress, and stopped dead in the middle of the room. She had clearly not meant to run this far. Behind her in the doorway appeared a university student with a crimson collar, a Guards officer, a fifteen-year-old girl, and a plump, rosy-faced boy in a short jacket.
The count leapt to his feet and, swaying side to side, threw his arms wide open around the little girl who had come running in.
"There she is!" he cried, laughing. "My darling, the birthday girl! My sweetheart!"
"My dear, there is a time and place for everything," the countess said with pretended sternness. "You spoil her, Ilya," she added, turning to her husband.
"How do you do, my dear? Happy name day to you," said the visitor. "What a delightful child," she added, turning to the mother.

This black-eyed, wide-mouthed girl — not pretty, but bursting with life — with her childish bare shoulders still heaving from running, her bodice shaking, black curls tossed back, thin bare arms, little legs in lace-trimmed drawers, and feet in low slippers — was at that enchanting age when a girl is no longer a child but not yet a young woman. Breaking free from her father, she ran to bury her flushed face in the lace of her mother's shawl, completely ignoring the stern remark, and began to laugh. Through broken sentences she tried to explain something about a doll she pulled from the folds of her dress.

"Look!... My doll... Mimi... Look..." was all Natasha could manage to say — everything struck her as hilarious. She leaned against her mother and burst into such a loud, ringing fit of laughter that even the prim visitor couldn't help joining in.
"Now then, off you go and take your little monster with you," said the mother, pushing her daughter away with mock severity, and turning to the visitor she added: "She's my youngest."
Natasha raised her face from her mother's shawl for a moment, glanced up through tears of laughter, and buried her face again.
The visitor, forced to witness this family scene, felt obliged to take some part in it.
"Tell me, my dear," she said to Natasha, "is Mimi a relation of yours? A daughter, I suppose?"
Natasha didn't like the visitor's condescending tone toward childish things. She made no reply and just looked at her seriously.

Meanwhile the younger generation — Boris, the officer, Anna Mikhaylovna's son; Nicholas, the university student, the count's eldest son; Sonya, the count's fifteen-year-old niece; and little Petya, his youngest boy — had all settled into the drawing room and were clearly trying to contain the excitement and laughter shining in all their faces within the bounds of good manners. Obviously the conversation in the back rooms, from which they had burst out so eagerly, had been far more entertaining than the drawing room talk of society scandals, weather, and Countess Apraksina. Now and then they glanced at each other, barely able to hold back their laughter.

The two young men, the student and the officer, childhood friends, were the same age and both good-looking, though quite different. Boris was tall and fair, with a calm, handsome face and regular, refined features. Nicholas was shorter, with curly hair and an open expression. Dark hairs were already showing above his lip, and his whole face radiated energy and enthusiasm. Nicholas blushed when he entered the drawing room. He obviously tried to think of something to say but couldn't. Boris, on the other hand, found his footing immediately and began telling — calmly and with humor — how he had known the doll Mimi when she was still quite a young lady, before her nose was broken, how she had aged in the five years he'd known her, and how her head had cracked right across the skull. As he spoke he glanced at Natasha. She turned away from him and looked at her younger brother, who was screwing up his eyes and shaking with suppressed laughter, and, unable to hold herself back any longer, she leapt up and dashed from the room as fast as her nimble little feet could carry her. Boris did not laugh.
"You were about to go out, weren't you, Mama? Shall I have the carriage brought round?" he asked his mother with a smile.
"Yes, yes, go and tell them to get it ready," she replied, returning his smile.
Boris quietly left the room and went to find Natasha. The plump boy ran after them, annoyed that their plans had been disrupted.

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Pierre knew this large room well—divided by columns and an arch, its walls hung with Persian carpets. The area behind the columns, with a tall silk-curtained mahogany bed on one side and an enormous icon case on the other, was bathed in red light like a Russian church during evening services. Beneath the gleaming icons stood a long reclining chair, and in it, propped on smooth white pillows that had obviously just been changed, Pierre saw the familiar, majestic figure of his father, Count Bezukhov—covered to the waist by a bright green quilt, with that gray mane of hair above his broad forehead that always made one think of a lion, and the deep, noble wrinkles of his handsome, ruddy face. He lay directly beneath the icons, his large, thick hands resting on top of the quilt. A wax taper had been placed between the forefinger and thumb of his right hand, which lay palm-down, and an old servant standing behind the chair held it in place. By the chair stood the priests, their long hair falling over magnificent, glittering vestments, holding lighted tapers and slowly, solemnly conducting the service. A little behind them stood the two younger princesses, holding handkerchiefs to their eyes. In front of them their eldest sister, Catiche, stood with a fierce and resolute expression fixed on the icons, as if declaring to everyone that she could not be held responsible for what might happen if she looked away. Anna Mikhaylovna stood by the door with a meek, sorrowful, all-forgiving expression, near the unfamiliar lady. Prince Vasili stood at the front, near the reclining chair, a wax taper in his left hand, his left arm resting on the carved back of a velvet chair he had turned around for the purpose, crossing himself with his right hand and raising his eyes heavenward each time his fingers touched his forehead. His face wore a look of calm piety and submission to God's will. "If you don't understand these feelings," his expression seemed to say, "so much the worse for you."

Behind him stood the aide-de-camp, the doctors, and the manservants. The men and women had separated as in a church. Everyone crossed themselves silently, and the only sounds were the reading of the service, the muffled chanting of deep bass voices, and in the pauses, sighs and the shuffling of feet. Anna Mikhaylovna, with an air of importance showing she knew exactly what she was doing, crossed the room to Pierre and handed him a taper. He lit it and, distracted by watching those around him, began crossing himself with the hand that held the candle.

Sophie, the rosy, youngest princess with the mole—the one who was always laughing—watched him. She smiled, buried her face in her handkerchief, and kept it hidden for a moment. Then she looked up, saw Pierre again, and couldn't help laughing once more. She clearly couldn't look at him without laughing, yet couldn't resist looking. To remove herself from temptation, she slipped quietly behind one of the columns. In the middle of the service, the priests' voices suddenly stopped. They whispered to each other, and the old servant holding the count's hand stood up and said something to the ladies. Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward and, bending over the dying man, beckoned to Lorrain from behind her back. The French doctor had no taper; he was leaning against one of the columns in a respectful posture that showed he—a foreigner—despite all differences of faith, fully understood the significance of the rite being performed and even approved of it. He now approached the sick man with the noiseless step of a person in full health, lifted the hand that lay free from the green quilt with his delicate white fingers, turned slightly to one side, and felt the pulse, reflecting for a moment. The sick man was given something to drink. There was a brief commotion around him, then everyone returned to their places and the service continued. During this pause, Pierre noticed that Prince Vasili left the chair he had been leaning on and—with an air suggesting that he knew what he was doing, and if others didn't understand, that was their problem—walked past the dying man without stopping, joined the eldest princess, and moved with her to the side of the room where the tall bed stood with its silk hangings. They both slipped out through a back door, then returned to their places one after the other before the service concluded. Pierre paid no more attention to this than to anything else going on around him, having decided once and for all that whatever was happening that evening was somehow essential.

The chanting stopped, and the priest's voice was heard respectfully congratulating the dying man on having received the sacrament. The dying man lay as lifeless and motionless as before. People began to stir around him—footsteps, whispers—among which Anna Mikhaylovna's voice was the most audible.
Pierre heard her say:
"He really must be moved to the bed. It's impossible here..."

The sick man was so surrounded by doctors, princesses, and servants that Pierre could no longer see the ruddy, yellowish face with its gray mane—though he hadn't lost sight of it for a single moment during the entire service, even while watching other faces. He could tell from the careful movements of those crowded around the reclining chair that they were lifting the dying man and carrying him.

"Hold onto my arm or you'll drop him!" one of the servants said in a frightened whisper. "Get a grip from underneath. Here!" voices called out, and the heavy breathing of the bearers and the scraping of their feet grew more urgent, as though the weight they carried was too much for them.

As the bearers—among them Anna Mikhaylovna—passed the young man, he caught a momentary glimpse between their heads and shoulders of the dying man's broad, uncovered chest and powerful shoulders, raised by those gripping him under the arms, and of his gray, curly, lion-like head. That head, with its remarkably wide brow and cheekbones, its handsome, sensual mouth, and its cold, majestic expression, was not disfigured by the approach of death. It looked just as Pierre remembered it from three months earlier, when the count had sent him to Petersburg. But now the head swayed helplessly with the uneven movements of the bearers, and those cold, indifferent eyes were fixed on nothing.

After a few minutes of commotion around the tall bed, the bearers dispersed. Anna Mikhaylovna touched Pierre's hand and said, "Come." Pierre went with her to the bed where the sick man had been laid in a stately pose befitting the ceremony just completed. He lay with his head propped high on the pillows, his hands placed symmetrically on the green silk quilt, palms down. When Pierre approached, the count was gazing straight at him—but with an expression whose meaning no living person could decipher. Either the look meant nothing at all, just that eyes must look somewhere as long as they exist, or it meant far too much. Pierre hesitated, unsure what to do, and glanced at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna made a quick gesture with her eyes toward the sick man's hand, moving her lips as if sending it a kiss. Pierre carefully craned his neck, trying not to touch the quilt, and pressed his lips to the large, fleshy hand with its heavy bones. Neither the hand nor a single muscle of the count's face moved. Pierre looked again at Anna Mikhaylovna, asking what to do next. She indicated a chair beside the bed with her eyes. Pierre sat down obediently, his expression silently asking whether he was doing the right thing. Anna Mikhaylovna nodded her approval. Once again Pierre assumed the naively symmetrical pose of an Egyptian statue, clearly distressed that his large, clumsy body took up so much space, doing his best to appear as small as possible. He looked at the count, who still stared at the spot where Pierre's face had been before he sat down. Anna Mikhaylovna's manner conveyed her awareness of the solemn importance of these final moments between father and son. This lasted about two minutes, though to Pierre it felt like an hour. Suddenly the broad muscles of the count's face began to twitch. The twitching grew stronger, the handsome mouth was pulled to one side—and only now did Pierre grasp how close his father was to death—and from that distorted mouth came a faint, hoarse sound. Anna Mikhaylovna watched the sick man's eyes intently, trying to read what he wanted. She pointed first to Pierre, then to a drink, then whispered Prince Vasili's name inquiringly, then pointed to the quilt. The dying man's eyes and face showed impatience. He made an effort to look at the servant who stood at the head of the bed.
"He wants to be turned onto his other side," the servant whispered, and rose to turn the count's heavy body toward the wall.
Pierre got up to help.

As the count was being turned, one of his arms fell back limply, and he made a futile effort to pull it forward. Whether he noticed the look of horror with which Pierre stared at that lifeless arm, or whether some other thought crossed his dying mind, he glanced at the disobedient arm, then at Pierre's terrified face, then back at the arm, and a faint, pitiful smile appeared on his face—completely at odds with his features—as though mocking his own helplessness. At the sight of that smile, Pierre felt an unexpected tremor in his chest and a prickling in his nose, and tears blurred his eyes. The sick man was turned onto his side, facing the wall. He sighed.
"He's dozing," said Anna Mikhaylovna, noticing one of the princesses coming to take her turn at the bedside watch. "Let's go."
Pierre went out.

title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The last of the infantry hurried across the bridge, bunching tighter as they neared it, as if squeezing through a funnel. Finally all the baggage wagons had crossed, the crowding eased, and the last battalion reached the bridge. Now only Denisov's squadron of hussars remained on the far side, facing the enemy. The French could be seen from the hill on the opposite bank but were not yet visible from the bridge itself, because the horizon as viewed from the river valley was formed by rising ground barely half a mile away. At the foot of the hill stretched wasteland where a few groups of Cossack scouts were moving about. Then suddenly, on the road at the top of the high ground, artillery and troops in blue uniforms appeared. These were the French. A group of Cossack scouts trotted back down the hill. All the officers and men of Denisov's squadron tried to talk about other things and look elsewhere, but every one of them was thinking only about what was up on that hilltop, and they kept glancing at the shapes appearing on the skyline—shapes they knew to be enemy troops. The weather had cleared again since midday, and the sun was sinking brightly over the Danube and the dark hills surrounding it. It was quiet, and at intervals the sound of bugle calls and shouting from the enemy drifted down from the hill. Between the squadron and the enemy there was now nothing but a handful of scattered skirmishers. An empty stretch of about seven hundred yards was all that separated them. The enemy had stopped firing, and that stern, menacing, untouchable line dividing two hostile armies could be felt more sharply than ever.

One step beyond that invisible boundary—which feels like the line between the living and the dead—lies uncertainty, suffering, and death. And what is over there? Who is over there? Beyond that field, that tree, that sunlit rooftop? No one knows, but you want to know. You are afraid to cross that line, and yet you long to cross it, knowing that sooner or later you must, and that you will have to discover what lies on the other side—just as you will inevitably have to learn what lies beyond death. But you are strong, healthy, cheerful, and keyed up, surrounded by others who are just as excited and alive. That is what anyone thinks, or at least feels, when they come within sight of the enemy, and that feeling lends a special intensity and joyful sharpness to everything that happens in such moments.

On the high ground where the enemy stood, a puff of cannon smoke rose and a ball came whistling over the heads of the hussar squadron. The officers who had been clustered together rode off to their positions. The hussars carefully straightened their formation. Silence fell over the entire squadron. Every man watched the enemy ahead and the squadron commander, waiting for the order. A second cannonball flew past, then a third. They were clearly aiming at the hussars, but each ball whistled rapidly overhead and landed somewhere beyond. The hussars didn't turn around, but at the sound of each shot—as if on command—the whole squadron, with its rows of faces so alike and yet so different, rose slightly in the stirrups, held its breath while the ball passed, and then settled back. Without turning their heads, the soldiers stole glances at each other, curious to read their comrades' reactions. On every face, from Denisov's down to the bugler's, the same expression showed around the chin and mouth: a mixture of tension, irritation, and excitement. The quartermaster glared at his men as though threatening punishment. Cadet Mironov flinched every time a ball flew past. Rostov, on the left flank astride his horse Rook—a handsome animal despite its lame leg—wore the happy look of a schoolboy called up for an exam before a large audience, confident he's going to shine. He kept glancing around with a bright, clear expression, as if inviting everyone to notice how calm he was under fire. But despite himself, that same hint of something new and serious showed around his mouth too.
"Who's ducking over there? Cadet Miwonov! That's not wight! Look at me!" Denisov called out. Unable to stay still, he kept wheeling his horse back and forth in front of the squadron.

The black, hairy, snub-nosed face of Vaska Denisov, and his whole short, sturdy frame with its sinewy hand and stubby fingers gripping the hilt of his bared saber, looked just as it always did—especially toward evening when he'd emptied his second bottle. He was only redder than usual. With his shaggy head thrown back the way birds do when they drink, pressing his spurs ruthlessly into the flanks of his good horse Bedouin, sitting as if he were falling backward in the saddle, he galloped to the other end of the squadron and shouted in a hoarse voice for the men to check their pistols. Then he rode up to Kirsten. The staff captain, on his broad-backed, steady mare, came toward him at a walk. His face with its long mustache was as serious as ever; only his eyes were brighter than usual.
"Well, what do you think?" Kirsten said to Denisov. "It won't come to a fight. Watch—we'll pull back."
"The devil only knows what they're up to!" Denisov muttered. "Ah, Wostov!" he cried, catching sight of the cadet's bright face. "You've finally got your chance!"
He smiled approvingly, clearly pleased with the young man. Rostov felt completely happy. Just then the commander appeared on the bridge. Denisov galloped up to him.
"Your excellency! Let us attack them! I'll dwive them off!"

"Attack, indeed!" the colonel said in a bored voice, scrunching his face as though swatting away a fly. "And why are you standing here? Can't you see the skirmishers are pulling back? Lead the squadron out."

The squadron crossed the bridge and moved out of range without losing a single man. The second squadron, which had been in the front line, followed them across, and the last Cossacks withdrew from the far bank.

The two Pavlograd squadrons, having crossed the bridge, retired up the hill one after the other. Their colonel, Karl Bogdanich Schubert, rode up to Denisov's squadron and proceeded at a walking pace near Rostov, without taking any notice of him—even though this was their first encounter since the incident with Telyanin. Rostov, feeling that he was at the front and in the power of a man toward whom he now admitted he'd been in the wrong, kept his eyes fixed on the colonel's athletic back, his light-haired nape, and his red neck. It struck Rostov that Bogdanich was only pretending not to notice him, and that his real purpose was to test the cadet's courage. So he straightened up and looked around cheerfully. Then it seemed to him that Bogdanich was riding so close on purpose, to show off his own bravery. Next he imagined that the colonel would send the squadron on some desperate charge just to punish him—Rostov. And then he pictured how, after the charge, Bogdanich would approach him as he lay wounded and magnanimously extend the hand of reconciliation.

The high-shouldered figure of Zherkov, familiar to the Pavlograds since he'd only recently left their regiment, rode up to the colonel. After being removed from headquarters, Zherkov hadn't stayed with the regiment, claiming he wasn't fool enough to toil at the front when he could earn more rewards by doing nothing on the staff. He had managed to attach himself as an orderly officer to Prince Bagration. Now he came to his former commander with an order from the rear guard.
"Colonel," he said, addressing Rostov's enemy with an air of solemn gravity, glancing around at his former comrades, "there's an order to halt and set fire to the bridge."
"An order from whom?" the colonel asked sourly.
"I don't exactly know 'from whom,'" the cornet replied in a serious tone, "but the prince told me: 'Go and tell the colonel that the hussars must return at once and burn the bridge.'"

Behind Zherkov came another officer from the suite, riding up to the hussar colonel with the same order. After him, the stout Nesvitski came galloping up on a Cossack horse that could barely carry his weight.

"Colonel, what's going on?" he shouted as he approached. "I told you to set fire to the bridge, and now someone's gone and botched it. Everyone over there is in a panic and nobody can figure out what's happening."
The colonel deliberately halted the regiment and turned to Nesvitski.
"You spoke to me about inflammable material," he said, "but you said nothing about setting fire to it."

"But my dear sir," said Nesvitski, reining in and taking off his cap to smooth his sweat-dampened hair with his plump hand, "wasn't I telling you to burn the bridge after the inflammable material had been placed?"

"I am not your 'dear sir,' Mister Staff Officer, and you did not tell me to burn the bridge! I know my duty, and I make it my habit to follow orders strictly. You said the bridge would be burned—but who was supposed to burn it? I couldn't know that by divine inspiration!"
"It's always the same!" Nesvitski said with a wave of his hand. "How did you end up here?" he asked, turning to Zherkov.
"Same errand. But you're soaking wet! Let me wring you out!"
"You were saying, Mister Staff Officer..." the colonel continued in an offended tone.
"Colonel," the officer from the suite cut in, "you need to move quickly, or the enemy will bring up their guns for grapeshot."
The colonel looked silently at the suite officer, then at the stout staff officer, then at Zherkov, and he frowned.
"I vill ze bridge fire," he announced in a solemn tone, as if to declare that despite all the aggravation he was enduring, he would still do the right thing.

Striking his horse with his long, muscular legs as though the animal were to blame for everything, the colonel rode forward and ordered Denisov's squadron—the second, in which Rostov was serving—to return to the bridge.
"There it is—just as I thought," Rostov said to himself. "He wants to test me!" His heart clenched and the blood rushed to his face. "Let him see whether I'm a coward!" he thought.

Once again, the grave expression the men had worn under fire settled over every bright face in the squadron. Rostov kept watching his enemy, the colonel, closely, searching his face for confirmation of his suspicions. But the colonel never once glanced at Rostov and looked just as he always did at the front—solemn and stern. Then came the word of command.
"Quick! Quick!" several voices repeated around him.

Sabers catching on bridles and spurs jingling, the hussars hastily dismounted, none of them quite sure what they were supposed to do. The men were crossing themselves. Rostov no longer looked at the colonel—there was no time. He was terrified of falling behind the others, so terrified that his heart seemed to stop. His hand shook as he handed his horse off to an orderly, and he felt the blood pound against his chest. Denisov rode past him, leaning back and shouting something. Rostov saw nothing but hussars running all around him, their spurs catching and sabers clanking.
"Stretchers!" someone shouted behind him.

Rostov didn't stop to think about what that call meant. He just ran, trying to stay ahead of everyone. But right at the bridge, not watching his feet, he stepped into some sticky, trampled mud, stumbled, and fell on his hands. The others rushed past him.
"At both sides, Captain," he heard the colonel's voice. Bogdanich had ridden ahead and pulled up his horse near the bridge, his face triumphant and cheerful.

Rostov wiped his muddy hands on his trousers, looked at his enemy, and was about to run forward again, thinking the further ahead he got, the better. But Bogdanich, without looking at him or showing any sign of recognition, shouted:
"Who's running down the middle of the bridge? To the right! Come back, Cadet!" he shouted angrily. Then, turning to Denisov, who had ridden out onto the bridge planks to show off his courage:
"Why take unnecessary risks, Captain? You should dismount," he said.
"Every bullet has its target," Vaska Denisov replied, turning in his saddle.

Meanwhile, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite stood together out of range, watching—now the small cluster of men in yellow shakos, dark-green braided jackets, and blue riding trousers swarming around the bridge, and now what was approaching from the far side: blue uniforms and groups of men with horses, clearly recognizable as artillery.

"Will they manage to burn the bridge or not? Who'll get there first? Will they set it ablaze, or will the French get close enough for grapeshot and wipe them out?" Every man watching from the high ground above the bridge was asking himself these questions with a sinking heart, gazing at the bridge and the hussars in the bright evening light and the blue-coated troops advancing from the other side with bayonets and guns.
"The hussars are going to catch it!" Nesvitski said. "They're within grapeshot range now."
"He shouldn't have taken so many men," the officer from the suite remarked.
"That's true enough," Nesvitski agreed. "Two quick fellows could have done the job just as well."

"Ah, your excellency," Zherkov put in, his eyes fixed on the hussars but still wearing that guileless look that made it impossible to tell whether he was joking or serious. "How you look at things! Send two men? But then who would earn the Vladimir medal and ribbon? As it is, even if they do get peppered, the squadron can be put up for honors and he can win a ribbon. Our Bogdanich knows how things are done."
"There!" said the officer from the suite. "That's grapeshot."
He pointed to the French guns, whose limbers were being hurriedly detached and pulled away.

On the French side, a cloud of smoke rose from one of the gun positions, then a second and a third almost simultaneously. At the moment the first report reached them, a fourth flash was visible. Then two booms in quick succession, and a third.
"Oh! Oh!" Nesvitski groaned as if in sharp pain, grabbing the officer from the suite by the arm. "Look! A man's gone down! Down, down!"
"Two, I think."
"If I were Tsar, I would never go to war," Nesvitski said, turning away.

The French guns were hastily reloaded. The infantry in blue advanced toward the bridge at a run. Smoke appeared again in irregular bursts, and grapeshot crackled and rattled against the bridge. But this time Nesvitski couldn't see what was happening there—a dense cloud of smoke had risen from the bridge. The hussars had managed to set it on fire, and the French batteries were now shooting at them not to stop them, but simply because the guns were aimed and there were targets to hit.

The French managed to fire three rounds of grapeshot before the hussars made it back to their horses. Two of the rounds went wide, the shot sailing too high, but the last one landed in the middle of a cluster of hussars and knocked three of them down.

Rostov, preoccupied with his feelings about Bogdanich, had stopped on the bridge with no idea what to do. There was no one to cut down—he had always imagined battles with saber in hand—and he couldn't help burn the bridge since he hadn't brought any burning straw like the other soldiers. He just stood there looking around, when suddenly he heard a rattling sound on the bridge, like nuts being spilled, and the hussar nearest to him fell against the railing with a groan. Rostov rushed over with the others. Again someone shouted, "Stretchers!" Four men grabbed the hussar and began lifting him.
"Oh God! For Christ's sake, leave me alone!" the wounded man cried, but they lifted him anyway and placed him on the stretcher.

Nicholas Rostov turned away and gazed into the distance, as if searching for something—at the waters of the Danube, at the sky, at the sun. How beautiful the sky was: how blue, how calm, how deep! How bright and glorious the setting sun! How softly the distant waters of the Danube glittered! And more beautiful still were the far-off blue mountains beyond the river, the convent, the mysterious gorges, the pine forests veiled in mist at their summits... There was peace there, and happiness... "I would want nothing else, nothing at all, if only I were there," Rostov thought. "In me alone and in that sunshine there is so much happiness. But here... groans, suffering, fear, and this chaos and rush... Over there—they're shouting again, and again everyone is running somewhere, and I'll run with them, and it—death—is here, above me and all around me... One more instant, and I will never again see this sun, this water, that gorge!..."

At that moment the sun began to slip behind the clouds, and more stretchers came into view before Rostov. And the fear of death and of the stretchers, and the love of the sun and of life, all merged into a single feeling of nauseating dread.
"Oh Lord God! You who are in that heaven—save me, forgive me, and protect me!" Rostov whispered.
The hussars ran back to the men holding their horses. Their voices grew louder and calmer. The stretchers disappeared from sight.
"Well, fwiend? So you've had a taste of gunpowder!" Vaska Denisov shouted right above his ear.
"It's all over—but I'm a coward. Yes, a coward!" Rostov thought, and with a deep sigh he took Rook from the orderly—the horse was standing with one hoof resting—and began to mount.
"Was that grapeshot?" he asked Denisov.

"You bet it was!" Denisov cried. "You all worked like real heroes, and it's nasty business! A charge is good work—hacking away at the enemy! But this kind of thing is pure hell, with them shooting at you like you're a target."
Denisov rode up to a group that had gathered near Rostov, made up of the colonel, Nesvitski, Zherkov, and the officer from the suite.
"Well, it seems no one noticed," Rostov thought. And it was true. No one had paid any attention, because everyone understood the sensation that a cadet experiences under fire for the first time.
"Here's something for you to report," said Zherkov. "Watch—I'll get promoted to sub-lieutenant for this."
"Inform ze prince zat I ze bridge fired!" the colonel declared, triumphant and beaming.
"And if he asks about the losses?"

"A trifle," the colonel said in his deep bass voice. "Two hussars wounded, and one knocked out." He couldn't hold back a satisfied smile, and he pronounced the words "knocked out" with ringing clarity.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: At five in the morning it was still completely dark. The troops at the center, the reserves, and Bagration's right flank had not yet moved, but on the left flank the columns of infantry, cavalry, and artillery — the ones designated to descend the heights first, attack the French right flank, and drive it into the Bohemian mountains according to plan — were already up and stirring. The smoke from campfires, into which the soldiers were tossing everything they couldn't carry, stung their eyes. It was cold and dark. Officers were hurriedly drinking tea and eating breakfast; soldiers were munching on biscuits and stamping their feet to keep warm, gathered around the fires and feeding the flames with the remains of sheds, chairs, tables, wheels, barrels, and anything else they didn't need or couldn't take. Austrian column guides moved back and forth among the Russian troops, serving as harbingers of the advance. As soon as an Austrian officer appeared near a commanding officer's quarters, the regiment began to move: soldiers ran from the fires, shoved their pipes into their boots, stuffed their bags into carts, grabbed their muskets, and fell into rank. Officers buttoned their coats, buckled on their swords and pouches, and walked along the ranks shouting orders. The wagon drivers and orderlies harnessed the horses and loaded the carts. The adjutants, battalion commanders, and regimental commanders mounted up, crossed themselves, gave last instructions to the baggage handlers staying behind, and the monotonous thud of thousands of marching feet echoed into the darkness. The column moved forward without knowing where it was headed, unable — because of the dense crowds around them, the smoke, and the thickening fog — to see either the place they were leaving or the place they were going.

A soldier on the march is hemmed in and carried along by his regiment just as a sailor is by his ship. No matter how far he walks, no matter what strange, unknown, or dangerous places he reaches, the soldier is always surrounded by the same familiar things — the same comrades, the same formation, the same Sergeant Major Ivan Mitrich, the same company dog Jack, the same commanding officers — just as a sailor always sees the same decks, masts, and rigging. A sailor rarely cares about the latitude his ship is crossing, but on the day of battle — who knows how or from where — a solemn, grave note sounds through the moral atmosphere of an army, one that everyone can feel. It awakens an unusual curiosity in the men. On battle day, soldiers strain to look beyond the concerns of their own regiment; they listen hard, look around eagerly, and press each other for news of what's happening.

The fog had grown so thick that even as dawn approached, they couldn't see ten paces ahead. Bushes looked like enormous trees, and flat ground appeared to be cliffs and slopes. Anywhere, on any side, an enemy invisible at ten paces might appear. But the columns marched on and on through the same fog, going downhill and uphill, past gardens and fences, across unfamiliar terrain, and nowhere did they encounter the enemy. On the contrary, the soldiers gradually became aware that in front, behind, and on every side, other Russian columns were moving in the same direction. Every soldier felt reassured to know that wherever he was headed, many more of his own were going there too.
"Look — the Kursk regiment's gone past too," voices said in the ranks.
"It's amazing how many of our troops are here, lads! Last night I looked at the campfires — there was no end to them. Like Moscow!"

Although none of the column commanders rode along the ranks or spoke to the men (the commanders, as we saw at the council of war, were in a bad mood and unhappy with the whole affair, so they simply followed orders without trying to boost morale), the troops marched cheerfully, as they always do when heading into action, especially an attack. But after about an hour of marching through the dense fog, most of the men had to stop, and an uncomfortable sense that something had gone wrong began spreading through the ranks. It's very hard to explain how such an awareness spreads, but it does — surely, imperceptibly, and unstoppably, the way water seeps into a creek bed. If the Russian army had been fighting alone without allies, it might have taken much longer for this sense of mismanagement to become a general conviction. But since there were allies, the disorder was naturally blamed on the stupid Germans, and everyone became convinced that a dangerous mix-up had been caused by the sausage-eaters.
"Why have we stopped? Is the way blocked? Or have we already run into the French?"
"No, you can't hear them. They'd be shooting if we had."
"They were in such a rush to get us started, and now here we stand in the middle of a field for no reason. It's all those damned Germans and their bungling! Stupid idiots!"
"I'd have sent them out in front, but no — they're all crowded up behind us. And now we're standing here hungry."
"Any idea when we'll get clear? They say the cavalry is blocking the way," said an officer.
"Ah, those damned Germans! Don't even know their own country!" said another.
"What division are you?" shouted an adjutant, riding up.
"The Eighteenth."
"Then what are you doing here? You should have moved on long ago — now you won't get there before evening."
"What idiotic orders! They don't even know what they're doing themselves!" said the officer, and rode off.
Then a general rode past, shouting something angrily in a language that wasn't Russian.
"Tafa-lafa! No one can understand a word he's saying," said a soldier, imitating the general who had ridden away. "I'd shoot every one of them, the bastards!"
"We were ordered to be in position by nine, and we haven't even gotten halfway. Fine orders!" This complaint was being repeated all around.
And the energy with which the troops had set out began turning to frustration and anger at the stupid arrangements and at the Germans.

The cause of the confusion was this: while the Austrian cavalry was moving toward the left flank, the high command realized the center was too far separated from the right flank, and all the cavalry was ordered to turn back to the right. Several thousand horsemen had to cross in front of the infantry, which had no choice but to wait.

At the head of the column, an argument broke out between an Austrian guide and a Russian general. The general shouted that the cavalry must be halted; the Austrian protested that it wasn't his fault — the blame lay with the higher command. Meanwhile the troops stood around, growing listless and disheartened. After an hour's delay they finally moved forward again, descending the hill. The fog that was lifting on the heights was even thicker in the valley below. Up ahead in the fog, a shot rang out, then another — first at irregular intervals, trata... tat — then faster and more steadily, and the fighting at the Goldbach Stream began.

Having stumbled on the enemy unexpectedly down by the stream in the fog, hearing no words of encouragement from their commanders, with the sense of being late spreading through the ranks, and above all unable to see anything in front or around them in the dense mist, the Russians exchanged shots with the enemy halfheartedly, advancing and then halting, receiving no clear orders from officers or adjutants who were wandering around the fog in unfamiliar terrain, unable to find their own units. This was how the fighting began for the first, second, and third columns, which had descended into the valley. The fourth column, with Kutuzov, remained on the Pratzen Heights.

Below, where the battle was unfolding, the fog was still thick; on the higher ground it was clearing, but nothing could be seen of what was happening in front. Whether the entire enemy force was six miles away as assumed, or right there in that sea of mist, no one knew until after eight o'clock.

It was nine in the morning. The fog lay unbroken like an ocean below, but higher up at the village of Schlappanitz, where Napoleon stood surrounded by his marshals, it was completely clear. Above them stretched a pure blue sky, and the sun's enormous disk trembled like a vast, hollow, crimson buoy floating on the surface of that milky sea of mist. The whole French army — and Napoleon himself with his staff — was not on the far side of the streams and ravines of Sokolnitz and Schlappanitz, beyond which the allies had planned to take up position and begin the battle. They were on the near side, so close to the Russian forces that Napoleon could distinguish mounted men from those on foot with the naked eye. Napoleon, wearing the blue cloak from his Italian campaign, sat on his small gray Arab horse slightly ahead of his marshals. He gazed in silence at the hills that seemed to rise from the sea of mist, on which the Russian troops were moving in the distance, and he listened to the sounds of gunfire from the valley. Not a single muscle moved in his face — which in those days was still thin. His gleaming eyes were fixed intently on one point. His predictions were being confirmed. Part of the Russian force had already descended into the valley toward the ponds and lakes, and another part was leaving the Pratzen Heights — which he intended to attack and considered the key to the whole position. Through the mist he could see that in a hollow between two hills near the village of Pratzen, the Russian columns, their bayonets glinting, were streaming continuously in one direction toward the valley and disappearing into the fog one after another. From the intelligence he'd received the night before, from the sounds of wheels and footsteps his outposts had heard during the night, from the disorderly movement of the Russian columns, and from every other indication, he could see clearly that the allies believed him to be far off in front of them, that the columns moving near Pratzen were the center of the Russian army, and that this center was already weakened enough to be successfully attacked. But still he did not begin the engagement.

This was a momentous day for him — the anniversary of his coronation. Before dawn he had slept a few hours, and now refreshed, vigorous, and in high spirits, he had mounted and ridden out onto the field in that happy mood where everything seems possible and everything goes right. He sat motionless, looking at the heights visible above the mist, and his cold face wore that particular look of assured, self-satisfied happiness you see on the face of a boy who is deeply and happily in love. His marshals stood behind him, not daring to interrupt his thoughts. He looked from the Pratzen Heights to the sun emerging from the fog.

When the sun had fully risen above the mist and the fields and vapor glowed with dazzling light — as though he had been waiting for exactly this moment to begin — he drew the glove from his elegant white hand, made a signal to the marshals, and gave the order to attack. The marshals, accompanied by adjutants, galloped off in every direction, and within minutes the main body of the French army was surging rapidly toward the Pratzen Heights, which were being steadily emptied as Russian troops marched down into the valley on their left.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the Pratzen Heights, where he had fallen with the flagstaff in his hand, Prince Andrew Bolkonski lay bleeding heavily, unconsciously letting out a gentle, pitiful, childlike moan.
Toward evening he stopped moaning and became completely still. He had no idea how long he had been unconscious. Suddenly he felt alive again, aware of a burning, tearing pain in his head.

"Where is it, that vast sky I never knew until now, but saw today?" was his first thought. "And I never knew this suffering either," he thought. "Yes, I knew nothing, absolutely nothing until now. But where am I?"

He listened and heard the sound of horses approaching, along with voices speaking French. He opened his eyes. Above him was the same vast sky with clouds that had risen higher still, and between them shone an endless blue infinity. He did not turn his head and did not see those who, judging by the hoofbeats and voices, had ridden up and stopped near him.

It was Napoleon, accompanied by two aides-de-camp. Bonaparte, riding across the battlefield, had given final orders to strengthen the batteries firing at the Augesd Dam, and was now surveying the dead and wounded left on the field.
"Fine men!" Napoleon remarked, looking at a dead Russian grenadier who lay facedown with a blackened neck, one stiffened arm flung wide.
"The ammunition for the guns in position is exhausted, Your Majesty," said an adjutant who had come from the batteries firing at Augesd.

"Have some brought from the reserve," said Napoleon, and having walked on a few steps, he stopped before Prince Andrew, who lay on his back with the flagstaff dropped beside him. (The flag itself had already been taken by the French as a trophy.)
"That's a fine death!" said Napoleon, gazing at Bolkonski.

Prince Andrew understood that this was said about him and that it was Napoleon who said it. He heard the speaker addressed as Sire. But he heard the words the way one might hear the buzzing of a fly. Not only did they not interest him — he paid no attention to them at all and immediately forgot them. His head was burning, he felt himself bleeding to death, and he saw above him the distant, vast, everlasting sky. He knew it was Napoleon — his hero — but at that moment Napoleon seemed to him such a small, insignificant creature compared with what was happening now between himself and that vast infinite sky with its drifting clouds. At that moment it meant nothing to him who might be standing over him or what was said of him. He was only glad that people were near him, and he only wished they would help him and bring him back to life, which now seemed so beautiful, since today he had learned to see it so differently. He gathered all his strength, trying to stir and make a sound. He weakly moved his leg and let out a faint, sickly groan that aroused his own pity.
"Ah! He is alive," said Napoleon. "Lift this young man up and carry him to the dressing station."
Having said this, Napoleon rode on to meet Marshal Lannes, who, hat in hand, rode up smiling to the Emperor to congratulate him on the victory.

Prince Andrew remembered nothing more: he lost consciousness from the terrible pain of being lifted onto the stretcher, the jolting while being carried, and the probing of his wound at the dressing station. He did not regain consciousness until late in the day, when he was carried along with other wounded and captured Russian officers to the hospital. During this transfer he felt a little stronger and was able to look around and even speak.

The first words he heard on coming to his senses were from a French convoy officer, who said rapidly: "We must stop here: the Emperor will pass this way shortly, and it will please him to see these prisoners."
"There are so many prisoners today — nearly the whole Russian army — he's probably tired of them," said another officer.
"All the same! They say this one is the commander of all Emperor Alexander's Guards," said the first, pointing to a Russian officer in the white uniform of the Horse Guards.
Bolkonski recognized Prince Repnin, whom he had met in Petersburg society. Beside him stood a nineteen-year-old boy, also a wounded officer of the Horse Guards.
Bonaparte came galloping up and pulled his horse to a stop.
"Which is the senior?" he asked, seeing the prisoners.
They named the colonel, Prince Repnin.
"You are the commander of Emperor Alexander's Horse Guards regiment?" asked Napoleon.
"I commanded a squadron," replied Repnin.
"Your regiment fulfilled its duty honorably," said Napoleon.
"The praise of a great commander is a soldier's highest reward," said Repnin.
"I give it with pleasure," said Napoleon. "And who is that young man beside you?"
Prince Repnin named Lieutenant Sukhtelen.
After looking at him, Napoleon smiled.
"He's very young to come meddling with us."
"Youth is no obstacle to courage," Sukhtelen muttered in a failing voice.
"A splendid reply!" said Napoleon. "Young man, you will go far!"

Prince Andrew, who had also been brought forward before the Emperor's eyes to complete the display of prisoners, could not fail to attract his attention. Napoleon apparently remembered seeing him on the battlefield and, addressing him, again used the phrase "young man" that was connected in his memory with Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you, young man," he said. "How do you feel, mon brave?"

Though five minutes earlier Prince Andrew had been able to say a few words to the soldiers carrying him, now with his eyes fixed straight on Napoleon, he was silent. So insignificant at that moment seemed all the interests that consumed Napoleon, so petty did his hero himself appear with his trivial vanity and delight in victory, compared to the vast, fair, and kindly sky he had seen and understood, that he could not answer him.

Everything seemed so pointless and insignificant compared to the solemn chain of thoughts that weakness from blood loss, suffering, and the nearness of death stirred in him. Looking into Napoleon's eyes, Prince Andrew reflected on the insignificance of greatness, the unimportance of life which no one could understand, and the still greater unimportance of death, the meaning of which no living person could comprehend or explain.

The Emperor, without waiting for an answer, turned away and said to one of his officers as he left: "Have these gentlemen attended to and taken to my bivouac. Let my doctor, Larrey, examine their wounds. Farewell, Prince Repnin!" And he spurred his horse and galloped away.
His face glowed with self-satisfaction and pleasure.

The soldiers who had carried Prince Andrew had noticed the little gold icon Princess Mary had hung around her brother's neck, and they had taken it. But seeing how the Emperor favored the prisoners, they now hurried to return the holy image.
Prince Andrew did not see how or by whom it was put back, but the little icon with its thin gold chain suddenly appeared on his chest outside his uniform.

"It would be good," thought Prince Andrew, glancing at the icon his sister had hung around his neck with such feeling and devotion, "it would be good if everything were as clear and simple as it seems to Mary. How wonderful it would be to know where to seek help in this life, and what to expect after it, beyond the grave! How happy and at peace I would be if I could now say: 'Lord, have mercy on me!' But to whom should I say that? Either to a Power indefinable, incomprehensible, which I cannot even address, let alone put into words — the Great All or Nothing," he said to himself, "or to that God who has been sewn into this amulet by Mary! There is nothing certain, nothing at all — except the unimportance of everything I understand, and the greatness of something incomprehensible but supremely important."

The stretchers moved on. At every jolt he felt unbearable pain again; his fever rose and he became delirious. Visions of his father, his wife, his sister, and his future son, the tenderness he had felt the night before the battle, the figure of the insignificant little Napoleon, and above all the vast sky — these became the main subjects of his fevered imaginings.

The quiet domestic life and peaceful happiness of Bald Hills appeared before him. He was already enjoying that happiness when that little Napoleon had suddenly appeared with his unsympathetic expression of narrow-minded delight at others' misery, and doubts and torments had followed, and only the heavens promised peace. Toward morning all these dreams dissolved and merged into the chaos and darkness of unconsciousness and oblivion, which in the opinion of Napoleon's doctor, Larrey, was far more likely to end in death than in recovery.
"He is a nervous, bilious subject," said Larrey, "and will not recover."
And Prince Andrew, along with others who were fatally wounded, was left to the care of the local inhabitants.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Rostov's involvement in Dolokhov's duel with Bezukhov was smoothed over through the efforts of old Count Rostov, and instead of being demoted to the ranks as he'd expected, Nicholas was appointed adjutant to the governor-general of Moscow. As a result, he couldn't go to the country with the rest of the family and was kept in Moscow all summer by his new duties. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov grew very close to him during his convalescence. Dolokhov lay ill at his mother's home — she loved him passionately and tenderly — and old Mary Ivanovna, who had taken a liking to Rostov because of his friendship with her Fedya, often talked to him about her son.

"Yes, Count," she would say, "he is too noble and pure-hearted for this depraved world of ours. Nobody values virtue anymore — it seems like a reproach to everyone. Now tell me, Count — was it right, was it honorable, what Bezukhov did? And Fedya, with his noble spirit, loved him and still doesn't say a word against him. Those pranks in Petersburg when they played tricks on a policeman — didn't they do it together? And look! Bezukhov got off without a scratch while Fedya had to shoulder the whole burden. Think what he went through! Yes, he's been reinstated, but how could they not reinstate him? I doubt there were many sons of the fatherland out there as brave as he was. And now this duel! Have these people no sense of decency or honor? Knowing he's an only son, to challenge him and shoot so accurately! Thank God He had mercy on us. And what was it all about? Who doesn't have affairs these days? If he was so jealous — to my mind — he should have said something sooner, instead of letting it go on for months. And then to challenge him, counting on Fedya not fighting because he owed him money! How low! How contemptible! I know you understand Fedya, my dear Count — and believe me, that's why I'm so fond of you. Very few people truly understand him. He has such a noble, heavenly soul!"
Dolokhov himself, during his recovery, spoke to Rostov in a way no one would have expected.

"I know people think I'm a bad man!" he said. "Let them! I don't care about anyone except those I love. But the people I love, I love so fiercely I'd give my life for them — and everyone else I'd crush if they got in my way. I have a wonderful, priceless mother and two or three friends — you among them — and as for the rest, they only matter to me insofar as they're harmful or useful. And most of them are harmful, especially the women. Yes, my friend," he went on, "I've met loving, noble, high-minded men, but I've never yet met a woman — whether countess or kitchen maid — who wasn't mercenary. I haven't found that divine purity and devotion I look for in a woman. If I found someone like that, I'd give my life for her! But these..." and he made a gesture of contempt. "And believe me, if I still value my life, it's only because I still hope to find such a heavenly creature — someone who will transform, purify, and lift me up. But you don't understand that."
"Oh yes, I understand completely," answered Rostov, who was now fully under his new friend's influence.

In the autumn the Rostovs returned to Moscow. Early in the winter Denisov arrived too and stayed with them. The first half of the winter of 1806, which Nicholas Rostov spent in Moscow, was one of the happiest and most carefree times for him and the whole family. Nicholas brought many young men home to his parents' house. Vera was a striking girl of twenty; Sonya was a girl of sixteen with all the charm of a flower just opening; Natasha — half grown-up and half child — was sometimes childishly amusing, sometimes enchantingly girlish.

At that time the Rostov household was filled with the kind of romantic atmosphere typical of homes where there are very young and very charming girls. Every young man who visited — seeing those responsive, smiling young faces (smiling, no doubt, at their own happiness), feeling the eager energy around him, and hearing the bursts of song and music and the lighthearted, open chatter of girls ready for anything and full of hope — felt the same thing: a shared readiness to fall in love and an expectation that happiness was just around the corner.

Among the young men Nicholas brought to the house, one of the first was Dolokhov, whom everyone liked except Natasha. She nearly quarreled with her brother over him. She insisted that he was a bad person, that Pierre had been in the right in the duel and Dolokhov in the wrong, and furthermore that he was disagreeable and fake.

"There's nothing to understand," she declared with stubborn conviction. "He's cruel and heartless. Look — I like your Denisov, even though he's a wild one and all that — I still like him. So you see, I can judge people. But with this one, everything is calculated, and I don't like that. But Denisov..."

"Oh, Denisov is completely different," replied Nicholas, implying that even Denisov was nothing compared to Dolokhov. "You need to understand what kind of soul Dolokhov has — you should see him with his mother. What a heart!"
"Well, I don't know about all that, but I'm uncomfortable around him. And did you know he's fallen in love with Sonya?"
"That's nonsense..."
"I'm sure of it. You'll see."

Natasha's prediction turned out to be right. Dolokhov, who normally didn't seek out women's company, began visiting the house frequently, and the question of whom he was coming to see — though nobody spoke of it openly — was soon answered. He came for Sonya. And Sonya, though she would never have dared say it aloud, knew it and blushed bright red every time Dolokhov appeared.

Dolokhov often dined at the Rostovs', never missed a performance they attended, and went to Iogel's dance parties for young people, which the Rostovs always frequented. He was pointedly attentive to Sonya and looked at her in a way that made not only her blush but even the old countess and Natasha turn red when they noticed his gaze.
It was obvious that this strange, powerful man was under the irresistible spell of the dark, graceful girl who loved someone else.

Rostov noticed something new in Dolokhov's behavior toward Sonya, but he didn't try to figure out what these new dynamics meant. "They're always falling in love with somebody," he thought about Sonya and Natasha. But he wasn't as comfortable around Sonya and Dolokhov as before, and he spent less time at home.

In the autumn of 1806, talk of war with Napoleon had flared up again, even more intensely than the year before. Orders went out to raise recruits — ten men from every thousand for the regular army, plus nine from every thousand for the militia. Bonaparte was denounced everywhere, and in Moscow nothing was talked about but the coming war. For the Rostov family, the real significance of all these war preparations was that Nicholas refused to stay in Moscow and was only waiting for Denisov's leave to end after Christmas so he could return with him to their regiment. His approaching departure didn't stop him from enjoying himself — if anything, it added urgency to his pleasures. He spent most of his time away from home, at dinners, parties, and balls.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Soon after this, the dark chamber's door opened to admit not the Rhetor but Pierre's sponsor, Willarski, whom he recognized by his voice. To more questions about the firmness of his resolve, Pierre replied: "Yes, yes, I agree," and with a beaming, childlike smile — his fat chest bare, stepping unevenly and timidly in one slipper and one boot — he moved forward while Willarski held a sword against his bare chest. He was led from that room through winding passages and finally brought to the doors of the Lodge. Willarski coughed; the Masonic knock with mallets answered him; the doors opened. A bass voice (Pierre was still blindfolded) questioned him about who he was, when and where he was born, and so on. Then he was led somewhere still blindfolded, and as they walked he was told allegories about the trials of his pilgrimage, about holy friendship, the Eternal Architect of the universe, and the courage with which he should endure hardship and danger. During these wanderings, Pierre noticed that he was referred to now as the "Seeker," now as the "Sufferer," and now as the "Postulant," to the accompaniment of various knockings with mallets and swords. As he was being led up to some object, he sensed hesitation and uncertainty among his guides. He heard them whispering and arguing, with one insisting he should be led along a certain carpet. After that they took his right hand, placed it on something, and told him to hold a pair of compasses to his left breast with the other hand and repeat after someone who read aloud an oath of loyalty to the laws of the Order. The candles were then snuffed out and some spirit was lit — Pierre could tell by the smell — and he was told he would now see the lesser light. The blindfold was removed and, by the faint glow of the burning spirit, Pierre saw, as in a dream, several men standing before him wearing aprons like the Rhetor's and holding swords pointed at his chest. Among them stood a man whose white shirt was stained with blood. Seeing this, Pierre moved forward with his chest toward the swords, wanting them to pierce him. But the swords were drawn back, and he was immediately blindfolded again.

"Now you have seen the lesser light," a voice said. Then the candles were relit and he was told he would see the full light; the blindfold was removed once more and over ten voices said together: "Sic transit gloria mundi."

Pierre gradually began to recover himself and looked around the room and the people in it. Around a long table covered in black sat about twelve men in garments like those he had already seen. Some of them Pierre had met in Petersburg society. In the President's chair sat a young man he didn't know, with a distinctive cross hanging from his neck. On his right sat the Italian abbe whom Pierre had met at Anna Pavlovna's two years earlier. There were also a very distinguished dignitary and a Swiss who had formerly been a tutor at the Kuragins'. All maintained a solemn silence, listening to the President, who held a mallet in his hand. Set into the wall was a star-shaped light. On one side of the table was a small carpet with various figures worked into it; on the other stood something resembling an altar on which lay a Bible and a skull. Around it stood seven large candlesticks like those used in churches. Two of the brothers led Pierre to the altar, placed his feet at right angles, and told him to lie down, saying he must prostrate himself at the Gates of the Temple.
"He must first receive the trowel," whispered one of the brothers.
"Oh, hush, please!" said another.

Pierre looked around in confusion with his nearsighted eyes, and suddenly doubts arose. "Where am I? What am I doing? Aren't they laughing at me? Won't I be ashamed to remember this?" But these doubts lasted only a moment. Pierre glanced at the serious faces around him, remembered everything he had already been through, and realized he couldn't stop now. He was horrified at his own hesitation, and trying to revive his earlier feeling of devotion, he prostrated himself before the Gates of the Temple. And in fact the devotion returned even more strongly than before. After he had lain there for some time, he was told to rise, and a white leather apron like the others wore was put on him; he was given a trowel and three pairs of gloves, and the Grand Master addressed him. He was told to keep the apron white, as it symbolized strength and purity; of the unexplained trowel, he was told to use it to cleanse his own heart of vice and to smooth his neighbor's heart with patience. As for the first pair of gloves — men's gloves — he was told that Pierre could not know their meaning yet but must keep them. The second pair of men's gloves he was to wear at meetings. And finally, of the third pair — women's gloves — the Grand Master said: "Dear brother, these women's gloves are intended for you as well. Give them to the woman whom you honor above all others. This gift will be a pledge of your purity of heart to her whom you choose as your worthy companion in Masonry." After a pause he added: "But beware, dear brother, that these gloves do not adorn unclean hands." While the Grand Master spoke these last words, Pierre thought he grew embarrassed. Pierre himself grew even more flustered, blushed like a child until tears came to his eyes, and began looking around awkwardly. An uncomfortable silence followed.

This silence was broken by one of the brothers, who led Pierre to the carpet and began reading from a manuscript book an explanation of all the figures on it: the sun, the moon, a hammer, a plumb line, a trowel, a rough stone and a squared stone, a pillar, three windows, and so on. Then Pierre was assigned a place, shown the signs of the Lodge, told the password, and finally allowed to sit down. The Grand Master began reading the statutes. They were very long, and Pierre — overwhelmed by joy, nervousness, and embarrassment — could not follow what was being read. He only caught the last words, which stayed in his mind.

"In our temples we recognize no distinctions," read the Grand Master, "except those between virtue and vice. Beware of creating differences that may violate equality. Fly to a brother's aid whoever he may be; guide the one who strays; raise the one who falls; never bear grudge or hatred toward a brother. Be kind and courteous. Kindle in every heart the flame of virtue. Share your happiness with your neighbor, and let envy never dim the purity of that joy. Forgive your enemy; do not seek revenge except by doing him good. Thus, fulfilling the highest law, you shall recover traces of the ancient dignity you have lost."

He finished and, rising, embraced and kissed Pierre, who, with tears of joy in his eyes, looked around, not knowing how to respond to the congratulations and greetings that met him from all sides. He recognized no acquaintances but saw in all these men only brothers, and burned with eagerness to begin working alongside them.
The Grand Master rapped with his mallet. All the Masons sat down in their places, and one of them read a sermon on the necessity of humility.

The Grand Master proposed that the final duty be performed, and the distinguished dignitary who held the title of "Collector of Alms" went round to all the brothers. Pierre wanted to give everything he had, but fearing it might look like pride, he contributed the same amount as the others.
The meeting was over, and on reaching home Pierre felt as if he had returned from a long journey lasting decades — completely transformed, having left behind his former habits and way of life.
